title: Analog quantum simulation of $φ^4$ field theory with a superconducting transmission line
authors: Ilan T. Rosen, Neill C. Warrington, Max Hays, Christopher McNally, Joshua Lin, Stephen Sorokanich, Julian Bender
abstract: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum fields remains a fundamental challenge. We propose a superconducting transmission line for analog quantum simulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional $φ^4$ field theory. The transmission line comprises fluxonium-like circuit elements whose continuous and unbounded phase variables encode a scalar field without Hilbert-space truncation. Their anharmonic potentials provide strong interactions. Tuning the circuit parameters provides access to two distinct regimes. In the first, the transmission line emulates $φ^4$ field theory with a single-well potential. We confirm this correspondence through lattice Monte Carlo calculations of the low-energy spectra of both the circuit and lattice $φ^4$ theory. This regime enables scattering experiments between counter-propagating particle wave packets. The second parameter set yields a double-well potential that emulates $φ^4$ theory in the symmetry-broken phase and hosts degenerate vacua. Interfaces between the two vacua form topological kinks, and the transmission line can simulate kink-antikink collisions. We present state preparation and measurement protocols for both collision experiments, enabling spatially resolved, real-time studies of particle and soliton scattering in an interacting quantum field theory.
summary: This paper proposes using a superconducting transmission line as an analog quantum simulator for $(1+1)$-dimensional $\phi^4$ field theory. By tuning circuit parameters, the system can mimic both simple particle scattering (single-well) and complex topological dynamics like kink-antikink collisions (double-well). This offers a powerful, experimentally accessible platform for studying interacting quantum field dynamics.
main_problem: The core challenge is understanding the real-time dynamics of strongly interacting quantum field theories, which is difficult using current computational or experimental methods.
main_result: The superconducting transmission line successfully emulates $(1+1)$-dimensional $\phi^4$ field theory, allowing for the simulation of both particle scattering and topological kink-antikink collisions.
method: The authors use analog quantum simulation by engineering a superconducting circuit whose time evolution mimics the field theory dynamics, validated by lattice Monte Carlo calculations.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a Non-linear Transmission Line (NLTL) built from fluxonium-like superconducting circuits. This system is tuned to emulate the Lagrangian of a $\phi^4$ field theory, allowing access to both single-well and symmetry-broken double-well potentials.
key_observables: Scattering cross-sections for particle wave packets, and the dynamics of topological kinks and anti-kinks.
important_parameters: The ratio of circuit parameters ($E_{JA}/E_J$ vs $n$) controls the potential regime (single-well vs. double-well). The simulation requires the continuum limit approximation.
main_assumptions: The method relies on the ability to fabricate a sufficiently large, controlled superconducting circuit, and approximations are used to derive the effective continuum action.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the free-field structure, the nonlinear circuit components, the resulting potential wells (single-well and double-well), and the convergence of the dispersion relation to the continuum theory.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system (NLTL) and its Hamiltonian, confirms its equivalence to the continuum $\phi^4$ theory via lattice calculations, and then details how tuning parameters allows access to different physical regimes (single-well for scattering, double-well for solitons).
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, hardware-based realization of simulating complex, interacting quantum field theories, bridging superconducting circuit QED with fundamental condensed matter physics problems.
